slides.body: That is where the 🔴 command comes in.
How to recover: push the old commits back from a clone that still has them.
Review practice. In one sentence: a review is a claim about a specific diff at a specific commit, so a good reviewer controls which diff and which commit they looked at.
As an author. Keep the pull request small.
As a reviewer. For anything risky, run the code: gh pr checkout, then the tests.
What a review cannot see: semantic conflicts with other open pull requests, files hidden by diff limits, and anything the test merge did not include.
Display limits. In one sentence: GitHub truncates large pull requests.

lines.s: # Asha, a maintainer of upstream, takes the pull request into her clone:

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Committing on the fork's default branch. Root cause: that branch can then no longer be fast-forwarded to upstream, and every later pull request from a branch based on it carries the stray commits.
Branching from the fork's main without fetching upstream. Root cause: the fork's main is as old as the last sync; the pull request range is taken against upstream.
Running gh repo sync --force to fix a fork that is ahead. Root cause: with --force the sync is a hard reset and discards the commits upstream does not have.
Pushing to a pull request branch after a maintainer edited it, without pulling. Root cause: the branch in your fork moved; your push is a non-fast-forward.
Approving a large pull request from the web page alone. Root cause: the page truncates beyond its display limits; the Git data is complete and git diff --stat base...head has no ceiling.

A maintainer fetches the pull request ref and, if allowed, pushes to your branch in your fork.
After the merge: fetch upstream, fast-forward main, push it to the fork; never commit on the fork's main.
A review is a claim about a diff at a commit; beyond the display limits, review with Git.

slides.body: Read sections 17.15, 17.17 and 17.18 of Chapter 17.
You can now walk a change from fork to merge and back, and rescue a fork that drifted.

beats.text: A contributor's third pull request to an open-source evaluation library shows eleven commits. She wrote one. The maintainer asks her to clean it up. She opens her fork, her own copy of the repository on GitHub, and finds that its main is three commits ahead of upstream, the original project, and forty-one behind. She never meant to commit on main. The page offers to sync, and a search result suggests gh repo sync --force.
beats.tele: A contributor's third pull request to an open-source evaluation library shows eleven commits. She wrote one. The maintainer asks her to clean it up. She opens her fork, her own copy of the repository on GitHub, and finds that its `main` is three commits ahead of upstream, the original project, and forty-one behind. She never meant to commit on `main`. The page offers to sync, and a search result suggests `gh repo sync --force`.

beats.text: A colleague who has done this before stops her: what happens to the three commits if you do that?
beats.tele: A colleague who has done this before stops her: what happens to the three commits if you do that?

beats.text: They are discarded. This video walks the fork workflow from end to end, so that the fork's main never gets into that state, and shows how to keep the stray work when it does. Keep those three commits in mind. Before the end, we get them back.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. You already have every piece of this. In the remotes videos you built the triangular configuration: origin is your fork, upstream the shared repository. In video 116 you saw what a fork is on the platform. In the last four videos you learned what a pull request is. This video puts the pieces in order, as one cycle with eight steps.

beats.text: In one sentence: in the fork-and-pull model you push to a repository you own and ask the upstream repository to take the commits. The pull request, your proposal to merge, lives in the upstream repository.
beats.tele: In one sentence: in the fork-and-pull model you push to a repository you own and ask the upstream repository to take the commits. The pull request, your proposal to merge, lives in the upstream repository.

beats.text: Three repositories. Upstream, which a maintainer controls. Your fork, on the platform, which you control. And your clone, on your machine, with two remotes, two names for other repositories: origin is your fork, upstream is the shared repository.
beats.tele: Three repositories. Upstream, which a maintainer controls. Your fork, on the platform, which you control. And your clone, on your machine, with two remotes, two names for other repositories: `origin` is your fork, `upstream` is the shared repository.

beats.text: Try it now, thirty seconds, on paper: draw the three boxes, and write origin and upstream on the arrows that leave your clone. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Try it now, thirty seconds, on paper: draw the three boxes, and write `origin` and `upstream` on the arrows that leave your clone. I'll wait.

beats.text: Two arrows: origin goes to your fork, upstream to the shared repository.
beats.tele: Two arrows: `origin` goes to your fork, `upstream` to the shared repository.

beats.text: Platform facts first, from GitHub's reference pages. "You do not need permission from the upstream repository to push to a fork you created." A fork and its upstream share the same Git data, which you saw in video 116. The author can let maintainers push to the pull request branch.
beats.tele: Platform facts first, from GitHub's reference pages. "You do not need permission from the upstream repository to push to a fork you created." A fork and its upstream share the same Git data, which you saw in video 116. The author can let maintainers push to the pull request branch.

beats.text: That works only for forks owned by a user: "You cannot give push permissions to a fork owned by an organization." And for workflows triggered by a pull request from a fork, "secrets are not passed to the runner" except GITHUB_TOKEN, which "has read-only permissions". The Actions security videos explain why.
beats.tele: That works only for forks owned by a user: "You cannot give push permissions to a fork owned by an organization." And for workflows triggered by a pull request from a fork, "secrets are not passed to the runner" except `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which "has read-only permissions". The Actions security videos explain why.

beats.text: The section ends with three rules, and the whole workflow follows from them. Never commit on the fork's default branch. Branch from upstream/main after a fetch. One branch per pull request, deleted after the merge.
beats.tele: The section ends with three rules, and the whole workflow follows from them. Never commit on the fork's default branch. Branch from `upstream/main` after a fetch. One branch per pull request, deleted after the merge.

beats.text: Why the first rule? Look at the three names in today's clone. The fork's main has one job: to be a copy of upstream's main. As long as it has no commits of its own, syncing it is a fast-forward, and a fast-forward cannot lose anything. The moment you commit there, a fast-forward is impossible, and every way of syncing either creates a merge commit on your fork's main, which then shows up in every later pull request, or discards your commits.
beats.tele: Why the first rule? Look at the three names in today's clone. The fork's `main` has one job: to be a copy of upstream's `main`. As long as it has no commits of its own, syncing it is a fast-forward, and a fast-forward cannot lose anything. The moment you commit there, a fast-forward is impossible, and every way of syncing either creates a merge commit on your fork's `main`, which then shows up in every later pull request, or discards your commits.

beats.text: Quick quiz. In the picture, the fork's main is one commit behind and has nothing of its own. Syncing it is: A, a fast-forward. B, a merge commit. C, a forced reset. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. In the picture, the fork's `main` is one commit behind and has nothing of its own. Syncing it is: A, a fast-forward. B, a merge commit. C, a forced reset. Your answer?

beats.text: A. The label slides forward along the line, and nothing can be lost.
beats.tele: A. The label slides forward along the line, and nothing can be lost.

beats.text: That is where the 🔴 command comes in. gh repo sync fast-forwards the fork's branch, and with --force it hard-resets it. The five answers. What it changes: a branch of the fork. What it can destroy: commits on that branch that upstream does not have. How to preview: git rev-list --left-right --count upstream/main...origin/main, which counts what each side has alone.
beats.tele: That is where the 🔴 command comes in. `gh repo sync` fast-forwards the fork's branch, and with `--force` it hard-resets it. The five answers. What it changes: a branch of the fork. What it can destroy: commits on that branch that upstream does not have. How to preview: `git rev-list --left-right --count upstream/main...origin/main`, which counts what each side has alone.

beats.text: How to recover: push the old commits back from a clone that still has them. When it is appropriate: when the fork's branch is meant to be an exact copy of its parent, which means after you have moved any stray work to a branch.
beats.tele: How to recover: push the old commits back from a clone that still has them. When it is appropriate: when the fork's branch is meant to be an exact copy of its parent, which means after you have moved any stray work to a branch.

beats.text: Review practice. In one sentence: a review is a claim about a specific diff at a specific commit, so a good reviewer controls which diff and which commit they looked at.
beats.tele: Review practice. In one sentence: a review is a claim about a specific diff at a specific commit, so a good reviewer controls which diff and which commit they looked at.

beats.text: As an author. Keep the pull request small. Check git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD before you open it. Say what you tested: for an ML change, which evaluation set, which metric, which commit. Once review has started, add commits instead of rewriting. If you must rewrite, say so, and keep the content change separate from the rebase.
beats.tele: As an author. Keep the pull request small. Check `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` before you open it. Say what you tested: for an ML change, which evaluation set, which metric, which commit. Once review has started, add commits instead of rewriting. If you must rewrite, say so, and keep the content change separate from the rebase.

beats.text: As a reviewer. For anything risky, run the code: gh pr checkout, then the tests. After a force push, compare the old and new series with git range-diff. Approve the commit you read. Give changes under .github/workflows/, to CODEOWNERS, to lock files and to deployment code a second reader. And treat an automated approval as a signal about the diff, not about the intent.
beats.tele: As a reviewer. For anything risky, run the code: `gh pr checkout`, then the tests. After a force push, compare the old and new series with `git range-diff`. Approve the commit you read. Give changes under `.github/workflows/`, to `CODEOWNERS`, to lock files and to deployment code a second reader. And treat an automated approval as a signal about the diff, not about the intent.

beats.text: What a review cannot see: semantic conflicts with other open pull requests, files hidden by diff limits, and anything the test merge did not include. Checks on the merged result catch those.
beats.tele: What a review cannot see: semantic conflicts with other open pull requests, files hidden by diff limits, and anything the test merge did not include. Checks on the merged result catch those.

beats.text: Display limits. In one sentence: GitHub truncates large pull requests. The Git data is complete, the page is not.
beats.tele: Display limits. In one sentence: GitHub truncates large pull requests. The Git data is complete, the page is not.

beats.text: The total diff of a pull request: 20,000 lines that you can load, or 1 megabyte of raw diff. One file's diff: 20,000 loadable lines or 500 kilobytes, of which 400 lines and 20 kilobytes load automatically. Files in one diff: 300. Commits listed on compare and pull request pages: 250, with a note that more exist.
beats.tele: The total diff of a pull request: 20,000 lines that you can load, or 1 megabyte of raw diff. One file's diff: 20,000 loadable lines or 500 kilobytes, of which 400 lines and 20 kilobytes load automatically. Files in one diff: 300. Commits listed on compare and pull request pages: 250, with a note that more exist.

beats.text: "Rebase and merge": 100 commits. Beyond a limit, review locally: git diff --stat base...head has no ceiling. A pull request that hits these limits is usually one of the cases from video 125, or a generated file that should not be in the diff.

beats.text: Think of the fork as your outbox on the platform. You do not write letters in the outbox. You write them at your desk, the clone, each on its own sheet, a branch. You put one sheet into the outbox and ask the recipient to take it. The outbox also holds a copy of the recipient's current rulebook, the fork's main, and you never write in that copy. You only replace it with the newer edition.
beats.tele: Think of the fork as your outbox on the platform. You do not write letters in the outbox. You write them at your desk, the clone, each on its own sheet, a branch. You put one sheet into the outbox and ask the recipient to take it. The outbox also holds a copy of the recipient's current rulebook, the fork's `main`, and you never write in that copy. You only replace it with the newer edition.

beats.text: The model breaks at one point, and you know it from video 116: a real outbox is yours alone. A fork shares its Git data with the whole network. What you put there is published, and stays reachable through upstream.
beats.tele: The model breaks at one point, and you know it from video 116: a real outbox is yours alone. A fork shares its Git data with the whole network. What you put there is published, and stays reachable through upstream.

beats.text: One: fork. Two: clone the fork. Three: fetch upstream, because the fork may already be behind. Four: push your branch to origin, the fork. Five: the pull request. Look at where the arrow lands: in the upstream box, as refs/pull/7/head. The pull request lives upstream, and so does a ref to your commit. Six: review round trips, in your clone. Seven: a maintainer merges. Eight: fetch upstream, fast-forward your main, push main to the fork.
beats.tele: One: fork. Two: clone the fork. Three: fetch upstream, because the fork may already be behind. Four: push your branch to `origin`, the fork. Five: the pull request. Look at where the arrow lands: in the upstream box, as `refs/pull/7/head`. The pull request lives upstream, and so does a ref to your commit. Six: review round trips, in your clone. Seven: a maintainer merges. Eight: fetch upstream, fast-forward your `main`, push `main` to the fork.

beats.text: Step eight is the one beginners skip.
beats.tele: Step eight is the one beginners skip.

beats.text: The count prints two numbers: commits only upstream has, and commits only your fork has. For a healthy fork that is merely behind, what must the second number be?
beats.tele: The count prints two numbers: commits only upstream has, and commits only your fork has. For a healthy fork that is merely behind, what must the second number be?

beats.text: Zero. Here: one and zero. Upstream has one commit your fork lacks, and the fork has nothing of its own.
beats.tele: Zero. Here: one and zero. Upstream has one commit your fork lacks, and the fork has nothing of its own.

beats.text: Start the branch from upstream/main, not from the fork's stale main.
beats.tele: Start the branch from `upstream/main`, not from the fork's stale `main`.

beats.text: --no-track keeps the branch from adopting upstream/main as its upstream. git push -u origin sets the fork's branch as the upstream branch. You could not push to upstream anyway.
beats.tele: `--no-track` keeps the branch from adopting `upstream/main` as its upstream. `git push -u origin` sets the fork's branch as the upstream branch. You could not push to upstream anyway.

beats.text: The commit is now stored in upstream, under refs/pull/7/head, on none of upstream's branches.
beats.tele: The commit is now stored in upstream, under `refs/pull/7/head`, on none of upstream's branches.

beats.text: Now the maintainer's side. Asha takes the pull request into her clone.
beats.tele: Now the maintainer's side. Asha takes the pull request into her clone.

beats.text: That is what gh pr checkout 7 does for her.

beats.text: She adds a test. Where can she push it so that it becomes part of your pull request?
beats.tele: She adds a test. Where can she push it so that it becomes part of your pull request?

beats.text: To your branch in your fork, which the maintainer-edit permission allows. Not to refs/pull/7/head: that ref is read-only.
beats.tele: To your branch in your fork, which the maintainer-edit permission allows. Not to `refs/pull/7/head`: that ref is read-only.

beats.text: Your branch moved without you. The log shows two authors on your pull request.
beats.tele: Your branch moved without you. The log shows two authors on your pull request.

beats.text: So pull before you add anything.
beats.tele: So pull before you add anything.

beats.text: Asha merges into upstream's main. Your main and your fork's main have not heard about it yet.
beats.tele: Asha merges into upstream's `main`. Your `main` and your fork's `main` have not heard about it yet.

beats.tele: Now step eight. Predict the two numbers the count will print when we're done. Say them out loud.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Committing on the fork's default branch. Root cause: that branch can then no longer be fast-forwarded to upstream, and every later pull request from a branch based on it carries the stray commits.
beats.tele: Committing on the fork's default branch. Root cause: that branch can then no longer be fast-forwarded to upstream, and every later pull request from a branch based on it carries the stray commits.

beats.text: Branching from the fork's main without fetching upstream. Root cause: the fork's main is as old as the last sync; the pull request range is taken against upstream.
beats.tele: Branching from the fork's `main` without fetching upstream. Root cause: the fork's `main` is as old as the last sync; the pull request range is taken against upstream.

beats.text: Running gh repo sync --force to fix a fork that is ahead. Root cause: with --force the sync is a hard reset and discards the commits upstream does not have.
beats.tele: Running `gh repo sync --force` to fix a fork that is ahead. Root cause: with `--force` the sync is a hard reset and discards the commits upstream does not have.

beats.text: Pushing to a pull request branch after a maintainer edited it, without pulling. Root cause: the branch in your fork moved; your push is a non-fast-forward.
beats.tele: Pushing to a pull request branch after a maintainer edited it, without pulling. Root cause: the branch in your fork moved; your push is a non-fast-forward.

beats.tele: A maintainer fetches the pull request ref and, if allowed, pushes to your branch in your fork.

beats.text: After the merge: fetch upstream, fast-forward main, push it to the fork; never commit on the fork's main.
beats.tele: After the merge: fetch upstream, fast-forward `main`, push it to the fork; never commit on the fork's `main`.

beats.text: A review is a claim about a diff at a commit; beyond the display limits, review with Git.
beats.tele: A review is a claim about a diff at a commit; beyond the display limits, review with Git.

beats.text: Read sections 17.15, 17.17 and 17.18 of Chapter 17.
beats.tele: Read sections 17.15, 17.17 and 17.18 of Chapter 17.

beats.text: You can now walk a change from fork to merge and back, and rescue a fork that drifted. Practise with Lab 21.1. Next: the three merge methods. Until then, look at the state first and type second. See you in the next one.
